Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache promises lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width, but on hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$, existing solvers fail catastrophically: unconstrained greedy and MCKP allocation achieve 32.45 and 36.92 perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B---far worse than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
We trace this failure to \emph{2-bit distortion compounding}: when the majority of heads are assigned 2-bit precision, per-head quantization errors interact non-additively through the residual stream, violating the additive objective assumed by standard solvers.
We show that a single cardinality constraint capping the number of 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, constrained allocation achieves 11.23 perplexity, a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint also renders solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce equivalent bit-width assignments across all three tested architectures ($\Delta{=}0.0000$), enabling use of a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm; per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality (max gap 0.02 PPL).
However, the benefit depends on architecture: on Llama-3.1-8B the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47), and on Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Notably, Yi-1.5-9B has the highest GQA ratio tested (8:1) and the highest top-5\% concentration (0.71), yet gains nothing from non-uniform allocation---because its heterogeneity is a single-outlier ``spike'' with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, rather than the ``spread'' pattern that enables MCKP to redistribute budget across heads.
We propose a joint diagnostic combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly identifies all five architectures studied---distinguishing spread heterogeneity (MCKP-exploitable) from spike and flat patterns where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We showed that per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding through the residual stream.
A single constraint---limiting simultaneously active 2-bit heads to $k \leq 8$ (7\% of heads)---reduces perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23, a 27.3\% improvement at $4\times$ compression.
Under the constraint, solver choice becomes irrelevant: greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all three architectures ($\Delta = 0.0000$), so a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm suffices.
The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on both the concentration and \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity.
Qwen2.5-7B (concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$, spread pattern) shows large gains; Llama-3.1-8B (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, spike) is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47 PPL); Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B show no benefit.
Yi-1.5-9B is a critical test case: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen), its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
A joint diagnostic using concentration ($\gtrsim 0.50$) and $t_1/t_5$ ratio ($\lesssim 0.70$) correctly identifies spread, spike, and flat patterns across all five models studied, computable from the same profiling pass used for allocation.
This provides a practical guideline: practitioners can determine whether non-uniform quantization is worthwhile for their architecture \emph{before} running the allocation solver.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Our study has several limitations that temper the generality of the findings.
First, we evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
Second, profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); alternative measures such as gradient-based or activation-norm diagnostics remain unexplored and could yield different allocation decisions.
Third, we report perplexity and downstream accuracy but no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
Fourth, we have not verified whether these findings transfer to larger scales (70B+), where head counts and attention patterns differ substantially.
Finally, although we validate on four downstream tasks, profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).

\paragraph{Future Work.}
Extending evaluation to 70B+ models would test whether the heterogeneity--benefit relationship holds at scale.
Integration with production inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) would enable real-kernel latency measurement, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) or dynamic per-request allocation could further improve the framework.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across five architectures at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
The mechanism is clear from the cross-bitwidth gradient structure.
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 has a 2-bit delta of 13.12, while the second-ranked head has delta 0.55---a $24\times$ gap ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$, $t_1/t_2{=}23.7$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's sensitivity is confined to the 2-bit operating point: its 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$.
The solver therefore has only one lever---upgrading L4H3 from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but further upgrading to 8-bit provides no additional benefit, so the budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go.
This is the ``spike'' pattern: high concentration driven by a single outlier with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.

In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth sensitivity gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern that enables meaningful budget reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

The remaining three architectures fill out the diagnostic picture.
Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Gemma-2-9B both exhibit flat distributions ($t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) with low concentration ($0.22$ and $0.23$ respectively), leaving the profiler with no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.15 vs.\ $+$0.13 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Head sensitivity heterogeneity and constrained allocation benefit across architectures at $4\times$ compression. $t_1/t_5$: ratio of top-1 to top-5 per-head 2-bit distortion (low${=}$spread, high${=}$spike). $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok); $^\ddagger$standard profiling, hires pending.}
\label{tab:heterogeneity}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Model & GQA & Top-5\% & $t_1/t_5$ & $\Delta$ PPL & $\Delta$ PPL & Shape \\
 & Ratio & Conc. & & (Uniform) & (Ours) & \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B & 7:1 & 0.61 & 0.57 & $+$5.64 & $+$1.42 & Spread \\
Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$ & 8:1 & 0.71 & 0.90 & $+$0.20 & $+$0.20 & Spike \\
Llama-3.1-8B$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.57 & 0.85 & $+$0.38 & $+$0.36 & Spike \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.22 & 0.18 & $+$0.10 & $+$0.13 & Flat \\
Gemma-2-9B$^\ddagger$ & 2:1 & 0.23 & 0.18 & $+$0.13 & $+$0.15 & Flat \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_head_delta_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Per-head 2-bit quantization sensitivity across five architectures. Qwen2.5-7B shows high concentration in Layer-0 heads (``spread'' pattern); Yi-1.5-9B shows a single extreme outlier at Layer-4 Head-3 (``spike'' pattern); Llama-3.1-8B shows a dominant outlier at Layer-2 Head-5 (49\% of total distortion, ``spike'' pattern); Mistral-7B-v0.3 shows near-zero sensitivity across all heads; Gemma-2-9B exhibits the most uniform distribution, consistent with its low GQA ratio (2:1). Color intensity indicates PPL increase when the head is quantized to 2-bit.}
\label{fig:heatmap}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the per-head 2-bit distortion as a heatmap.
The contrast is stark: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion (dark cells) while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero; Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (34\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform---a ``spike'' that MCKP cannot exploit; Gemma-2 exhibits the most uniform heatmap across its 336 heads, consistent with its 0.23 concentration; Mistral shows similarly low distortion across all layers and heads.

\subsection{Diagnostic Framework}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$, low $t_1/t_5$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. Mistral (0.22, $t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.18$): counterproductive.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.
Both thresholds are illustrative, derived from five models; they should be validated on a broader set before being treated as general rules.
The diagnostic adds no computational overhead: it reuses the profiling data already required for the allocation solver and avoids wasted optimization effort on architectures where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache promises lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width, but on hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$, existing solvers fail catastrophically: unconstrained greedy and MCKP allocation achieve 32.45 and 36.92 perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B---far worse than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
We trace this failure to \emph{2-bit distortion compounding}: when the majority of heads are assigned 2-bit precision, per-head quantization errors interact non-additively through the residual stream, violating the additive objective assumed by standard solvers.
We show that a single cardinality constraint capping the number of 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, constrained allocation achieves 11.23 perplexity, a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint also renders solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce equivalent bit-width assignments across all three tested architectures ($\Delta{=}0.0000$), enabling use of a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm; per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality (max gap 0.02 PPL).
However, the benefit depends on architecture: on Llama-3.1-8B the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47), and on Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Notably, Yi-1.5-9B has the highest GQA ratio tested (8:1) and the highest top-5\% concentration (0.71), yet gains nothing from non-uniform allocation---because its heterogeneity is a single-outlier ``spike'' with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, rather than the ``spread'' pattern that enables MCKP to redistribute budget across heads.
We propose a joint diagnostic combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly identifies all five architectures studied---distinguishing spread heterogeneity (MCKP-exploitable) from spike and flat patterns where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We showed that per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding through the residual stream.
A single constraint---limiting simultaneously active 2-bit heads to $k \leq 8$ (7\% of heads)---reduces perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23, a 27.3\% improvement at $4\times$ compression.
Under the constraint, solver choice becomes irrelevant: greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all three architectures ($\Delta = 0.0000$), so a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm suffices.
The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on both the concentration and \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity.
Qwen2.5-7B (concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$, spread pattern) shows large gains; Llama-3.1-8B (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, spike) is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47 PPL); Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B show no benefit.
Yi-1.5-9B is a critical test case: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen), its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
A joint diagnostic using concentration ($\gtrsim 0.50$) and $t_1/t_5$ ratio ($\lesssim 0.70$) correctly identifies spread, spike, and flat patterns across all five models studied, computable from the same profiling pass used for allocation.
This provides a practical guideline: practitioners can determine whether non-uniform quantization is worthwhile for their architecture \emph{before} running the allocation solver.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Our study has several limitations that temper the generality of the findings.
First, we evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
Second, profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); alternative measures such as gradient-based or activation-norm diagnostics remain unexplored and could yield different allocation decisions.
Third, we report perplexity and downstream accuracy but no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
Fourth, we have not verified whether these findings transfer to larger scales (70B+), where head counts and attention patterns differ substantially.
Finally, although we validate on four downstream tasks, profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).

\paragraph{Future Work.}
Extending evaluation to 70B+ models would test whether the heterogeneity--benefit relationship holds at scale.
Integration with production inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) would enable real-kernel latency measurement, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) or dynamic per-request allocation could further improve the framework.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Models.}
We evaluate on five architectures spanning different grouped-query attention (GQA) configurations:
\textbf{Qwen2.5-7B} (GQA ratio 7:1, 28 layers $\times$ 4 KV heads = 112 KV heads),
\textbf{Yi-1.5-9B} (8:1, 48 $\times$ 4 = 192 KV heads),
\textbf{Llama-3.1-8B} (4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256 KV heads),
\textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3} (4:1, 32 $\times$ 8 = 256 KV heads, sliding window attention),
and \textbf{Gemma-2-9B} (2:1, 42 $\times$ 8 = 336 KV heads, \texttt{head\_dim}=256, attention logit softcapping).
This selection spans GQA ratios from 2:1 to 8:1 and covers standard, sliding-window, and softcapped attention.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report perplexity (PPL, $\downarrow$) on the WikiText-2 test split (298{,}938 tokens) under bf16 inference with stride 512.
For downstream evaluation, we use ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande under 0-shot prompting.

\paragraph{Profiling.}
Per-head sensitivity is measured by independently quantizing each head to each candidate bit-width in $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ and recording the PPL increase over the bf16 baseline.
We use two profiling resolutions: \emph{standard} (16 sequences $\times$ 512 tokens) and \emph{high-resolution} (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens), both from WikiText-2 train.
Unless marked with $\dagger$, all results use standard-resolution profiling; Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution} analyzes the effect of resolution.

\paragraph{Compression and constraint.}
The default target is 4$\times$ compression (average 4 bits, budget ratio 0.25).
The cardinality constraint limits 2-bit assignments to at most $k$ heads, where $k$ is selected via the compounding sweep described in \S\ref{sec:method} ($k{=}8$ for Qwen, $k{=}2$ for Yi-1.5 and Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral, $k{=}8$ for Gemma-2).

\paragraph{Baselines.}
We compare against:
(1)~uniform 4-bit quantization;
(2)~unconstrained greedy allocation (RateQuant-style~\cite{zuo2026ratequant});
(3)~unconstrained MCKP allocation;
(4)~an L0-random heuristic that assigns Layer-0 heads to 8-bit and $k$ random non-Layer-0 heads to 2-bit, with remaining heads at 4-bit (5 seeds; we report mean$\pm$std and median);
and (5)~a naive positional heuristic that assigns Layer-0 to 8-bit and the $k$ deepest heads to 2-bit.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main_results}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small

Best constrained result per model in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok); standard profiling does not improve over uniform on these architectures. $^\ddagger$Best $k$ from ablation ($k{=}4$). The $\pm$0.06 on Qwen reports std over 3 calibration seeds (hires profiling); bit distributions are identical across seeds.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Model & Baseline & Uniform & \multicolumn{2}{c}{Unconstrained} & Ours \\
 & (bf16) & (4-bit) & Greedy & MCKP & (Constr.) \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B      & 9.81  & 15.45 & 32.45 & 36.92 & \textbf{11.23}$\pm$0.06 \\

Gemma-2-9B      & 8.90  & 9.03  & ---   & ---   & 9.05 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} summarizes the main results.
On Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP achieves 11.23 PPL, a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit (15.45).
Higher-resolution profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok) further improves this to 10.91; we report the standard-profiling result here and analyze the effect of profiling resolution in Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution}.
Without the cardinality constraint, both greedy (32.45) and MCKP (36.92) perform \emph{worse} than uniform---a catastrophic failure caused by excessive 2-bit assignments that compound across layers.
The constraint eliminates this failure mode entirely.
Across 3 calibration seeds, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL 10.99$\pm$0.06 (std is 1.3\% of the uniform gap), with 90.2\% three-way allocation agreement, confirming profiling stability.

On Llama-3.1-8B, the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47, $\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
Hires profiling reveals a spike pattern (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) dominated by a single top head (L2H5), leaving little cross-bitwidth gradient for non-uniform allocation to exploit.

On Mistral-7B-v0.3, constrained MCKP (7.16, $k{=}4$) is slightly worse than uniform (7.13, $+$0.4\%).
This is a genuine negative result: the profiler reports near-zero sensitivity differences across heads, meaning the optimization has no reliable signal to exploit.
Mistral's sliding-window attention may contribute to this uniformity by limiting head-level variation in effective context length.

On Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$, constrained MCKP ($k{=}2$) achieves 7.22 PPL, essentially identical to uniform 7.22 ($<$0.01\% difference).
Despite having the highest GQA ratio in our evaluation (8:1) and the highest concentration tested (0.71), Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier (Layer-4 Head-3, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$), a spike pattern that leaves no cross-bitwidth gradient for the solver to exploit.

On Gemma-2-9B (GQA 2:1), constrained MCKP ($k{=}8$) achieves 9.05 PPL vs.\ uniform 9.03---a 0.3\% degradation.
Gemma-2 has the most uniform head sensitivity distribution across its 336 KV heads, consistent with its low GQA ratio and attention logit softcapping.

Unconstrained results for Llama, Mistral, Yi-1.5, and Gemma-2 are omitted (---) as those experiments were conducted only on Qwen, where the failure mode is most pronounced.
Figure~\ref{fig:allocation} visualizes the bit-width allocation on Qwen, showing how constrained MCKP protects Layer-0 heads at 8-bit while selectively assigning only the 8 least-sensitive heads to 2-bit.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_allocation_comparison.pdf}
\caption{Bit-width allocation on Qwen2.5-7B at 4$\times$ compression. Uniform assigns all heads to 4-bit. Constrained MCKP protects Layer-0 heads at 8-bit and assigns the 8 least-sensitive heads to 2-bit.}
\label{fig:allocation}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Budget Sweep}
\label{sec:budget_sweep}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect of compression ratio on Qwen2.5-7B. Constrained MCKP provides meaningful gains at moderate-to-aggressive compression ($\geq$4$\times$). Standard-resolution profiling; hires results in Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution}.}
\label{tab:budget_sweep}
\begin{tabular}{cccc}
\toprule
Compression & Uniform PPL & Constr.\ MCKP PPL & $\Delta$ PPL \\
\midrule
2$\times$ & 10.10 & 10.66 & $-$0.56 \\
4$\times$ & 15.45 & 11.23 & $+$4.22 \\
8$\times$ & 14{,}759 & 907 & $+$13{,}852 \\

Table~\ref{tab:budget_sweep} shows how the benefit of constrained allocation varies with compression ratio on Qwen2.5-7B.

At 2$\times$ compression, uniform 8-bit quantization is near-lossless (10.10 PPL vs.\ 9.81 bf16, $+$0.29).
Per-head optimization has no headroom here; constrained MCKP is slightly worse (10.66) due to unnecessary 2-bit assignments that the budget permits but the model does not need.

At 4$\times$, the gap is substantial: constrained MCKP reduces PPL from 15.45 to 11.23, a 27.3\% improvement.
Hires profiling further reduces this to 10.91 (Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution}).

At 8$\times$, both methods degrade catastrophically---the budget is too aggressive for any allocation to preserve model quality.
However, constrained MCKP (907) is an order of magnitude better than uniform (14{,}759) because the constraint still protects Layer-0 heads at 8-bit, preventing total representational collapse.
Neither result is practically usable, but the gap demonstrates the protection mechanism at work.

\subsection{Heuristic Baselines}
\label{sec:heuristic}

\centering
\small
\caption{Constrained MCKP vs.\ heuristic baselines at 4$\times$ compression. L0-random reports median and mean$\pm$std over 5 seeds. All methods use per-model optimal $k$ ($k{=}8$ for Qwen, $k{=}2$ for Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral). Llama and Mistral use hires profiling, consistent with Table~\ref{tab:main_results}.}
\label{tab:heuristic}

\toprule
Model & MCKP & \multicolumn{2}{c}{L0-random} & Naive \\

\midrule

Llama-3.1-8B    & 8.45  & 8.62  & 8.62$\pm$0.07  & 8.58 \\

Table~\ref{tab:heuristic} compares profiling-guided MCKP against heuristic baselines that use the same Layer-0 protection but assign 2-bit heads without profiling.

On Qwen, MCKP (11.23) beats the L0-random median (11.52) by 0.29 PPL and the naive positional heuristic (12.23) by 1.00 PPL, confirming that profiling-guided selection outperforms both random and depth-based assignment.

On Llama ($k{=}2$), the gap between methods is small: MCKP achieves 8.45 vs.\ L0-random 8.62 and naive positional 8.58.
With only 2 heads assigned to 2-bit, the choice of which heads to compress has limited impact, and all methods cluster within 0.17 PPL.
MCKP still achieves the best result, but the practical advantage of profiling-guided selection is negligible at this constraint level.

On Mistral ($k{=}4$), all non-uniform strategies are worse than uniform 4-bit (7.13): MCKP 7.16, naive 7.21, L0-random median 7.20 (mean 7.24$\pm$0.07).
MCKP outperforms both heuristics, but the best non-uniform result (7.16) still exceeds uniform by 0.03 PPL, reinforcing that non-uniform allocation is counterproductive when heterogeneity is low.
Note that the heuristic baselines use a slightly higher budget (0.256 vs.\ 0.248 for MCKP, a 3\% difference) because integer $k$ does not divide evenly into the target; despite this advantage, they still underperform MCKP, making the comparison conservative.

Constrained MCKP improves average 0-shot accuracy by 2.6 points over uniform 4-bit (0.686 vs.\ 0.660), with gains on all four benchmarks.
The largest gain appears on HellaSwag ($+$4.0 pts), where language modeling quality is most directly reflected.

Constrained MCKP recovers approximately 73\% of the accuracy lost by uniform 4-bit quantization, indicating that per-head bit allocation addresses much of the degradation, though a gap to bf16 remains.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Stability}
\label{sec:cross_dataset}

To verify that the profiled allocation is not overfit to the calibration corpus, we profile on C4 and evaluate on WikiText-2, and vice versa, at $4\times$ compression.
On Qwen2.5-7B, C4-calibrated MCKP achieves 11.29 PPL on WikiText-2 (vs.\ 15.45 uniform, a 27\% reduction), only 0.06 PPL above the WikiText-2-calibrated result (11.23).
In the reverse direction, WikiText-2-calibrated MCKP achieves 20.56 PPL on the C4 held-out split (vs.\ 35.42 uniform, a 42\% reduction; C4 bf16 baseline on this split is 15.32).
All three models show ${>}96\%$ bit-assignment agreement across calibration sources: Qwen 96.4\% (108/112 heads), Llama 97.7\% (250/256), and Mistral 96.5\% (247/256).
Qwen's agreement is the most informative, as all 112 heads have variable assignments; on Llama, 253 of 256 heads are forced to 4-bit by the $k{=}2$ constraint, inflating agreement.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across five architectures at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
The mechanism is clear from the cross-bitwidth gradient structure.
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 has a 2-bit delta of 13.12, while the second-ranked head has delta 0.55---a $24\times$ gap ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$, $t_1/t_2{=}23.7$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's sensitivity is confined to the 2-bit operating point: its 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$.
The solver therefore has only one lever---upgrading L4H3 from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but further upgrading to 8-bit provides no additional benefit, so the budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go.
This is the ``spike'' pattern: high concentration driven by a single outlier with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.

In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth sensitivity gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern that enables meaningful budget reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

The remaining three architectures fill out the diagnostic picture.
Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Gemma-2-9B both exhibit flat distributions ($t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) with low concentration ($0.22$ and $0.23$ respectively), leaving the profiler with no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.15 vs.\ $+$0.13 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

\caption{Per-head 2-bit quantization sensitivity across five architectures. Qwen2.5-7B shows high concentration in Layer-0 heads (``spread'' pattern); Yi-1.5-9B shows a single extreme outlier at Layer-4 Head-3 (``spike'' pattern); Llama-3.1-8B shows a dominant outlier at Layer-2 Head-5 (49\% of total distortion, ``spike'' pattern); Mistral-7B-v0.3 shows near-zero sensitivity across all heads; Gemma-2-9B exhibits the most uniform distribution, consistent with its low GQA ratio (2:1). Color intensity indicates PPL increase when the head is quantized to 2-bit.}
\label{fig:heatmap}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the per-head 2-bit distortion as a heatmap.
The contrast is stark: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion (dark cells) while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero; Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (34\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform---a ``spike'' that MCKP cannot exploit; Gemma-2 exhibits the most uniform heatmap across its 336 heads, consistent with its 0.23 concentration; Mistral shows similarly low distortion across all layers and heads.

\subsection{Diagnostic Framework}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$, low $t_1/t_5$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. Mistral (0.22, $t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.18$): counterproductive.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.
Both thresholds are illustrative, derived from five models; they should be validated on a broader set before being treated as general rules.
The diagnostic adds no computational overhead: it reuses the profiling data already required for the allocation solver and avoids wasted optimization effort on architectures where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache promises lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width, but on hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$, existing solvers fail catastrophically: unconstrained greedy and MCKP allocation achieve 32.45 and 36.92 perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B---far worse than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
We trace this failure to \emph{2-bit distortion compounding}: when the majority of heads are assigned 2-bit precision, per-head quantization errors interact non-additively through the residual stream, violating the additive objective assumed by standard solvers.
We show that a single cardinality constraint capping the number of 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, constrained allocation achieves 11.23 perplexity, a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint also renders solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce equivalent bit-width assignments across all three tested architectures ($\Delta{=}0.0000$), enabling use of a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm; per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality (max gap 0.02 PPL).
However, the benefit depends on architecture: on Llama-3.1-8B the result is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47), and on Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Notably, Yi-1.5-9B has the highest GQA ratio tested (8:1) and the highest top-5\% concentration (0.71), yet gains nothing from non-uniform allocation---because its heterogeneity is a single-outlier ``spike'' with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, rather than the ``spread'' pattern that enables MCKP to redistribute budget across heads.
We propose a joint diagnostic combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly identifies all five architectures studied---distinguishing spread heterogeneity (MCKP-exploitable) from spike and flat patterns where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We showed that per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding through the residual stream.
A single constraint---limiting simultaneously active 2-bit heads to $k \leq 8$ (7\% of heads)---reduces perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23, a 27.3\% improvement at $4\times$ compression.
Under the constraint, solver choice becomes irrelevant: greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all three architectures ($\Delta = 0.0000$), so a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm suffices.
The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on both the concentration and \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity.
Qwen2.5-7B (concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$, spread pattern) shows large gains; Llama-3.1-8B (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, spike) is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47 PPL); Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B show no benefit.
Yi-1.5-9B is a critical test case: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen), its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
A joint diagnostic using concentration ($\gtrsim 0.50$) and $t_1/t_5$ ratio ($\lesssim 0.70$) correctly identifies spread, spike, and flat patterns across all five models studied, computable from the same profiling pass used for allocation.
This provides a practical guideline: practitioners can determine whether non-uniform quantization is worthwhile for their architecture \emph{before} running the allocation solver.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Our study has several limitations that temper the generality of the findings.
First, we evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
Second, profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); alternative measures such as gradient-based or activation-norm diagnostics remain unexplored and could yield different allocation decisions.
Third, we report perplexity and downstream accuracy but no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
Fourth, we have not verified whether these findings transfer to larger scales (70B+), where head counts and attention patterns differ substantially.
Finally, although we validate on four downstream tasks, profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).

\paragraph{Future Work.}
Extending evaluation to 70B+ models would test whether the heterogeneity--benefit relationship holds at scale.
Integration with production inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) would enable real-kernel latency measurement, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) or dynamic per-request allocation could further improve the framework.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across five architectures at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
The mechanism is clear from the cross-bitwidth gradient structure.
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 has a 2-bit delta of 13.12, while the second-ranked head has delta 0.55---a $24\times$ gap ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$, $t_1/t_2{=}23.7$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's sensitivity is confined to the 2-bit operating point: its 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$.
The solver therefore has only one lever---upgrading L4H3 from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but further upgrading to 8-bit provides no additional benefit, so the budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go.
This is the ``spike'' pattern: high concentration driven by a single outlier with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.

In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth sensitivity gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern that enables meaningful budget reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

The remaining three architectures fill out the diagnostic picture.
Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Gemma-2-9B both exhibit flat distributions ($t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) with low concentration ($0.22$ and $0.23$ respectively), leaving the profiler with no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.15 vs.\ $+$0.13 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Head sensitivity heterogeneity and constrained allocation benefit across architectures at $4\times$ compression. $t_1/t_5$: ratio of top-1 to top-5 per-head 2-bit distortion (low${=}$spread, high${=}$spike). $^\dagger$Hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok); $^\ddagger$standard profiling, hires pending.}
\label{tab:heterogeneity}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
Model & GQA & Top-5\% & $t_1/t_5$ & $\Delta$ PPL & $\Delta$ PPL & Shape \\
 & Ratio & Conc. & & (Uniform) & (Ours) & \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B & 7:1 & 0.61 & 0.57 & $+$5.64 & $+$1.42 & Spread \\
Yi-1.5-9B$^\dagger$ & 8:1 & 0.71 & 0.90 & $+$0.20 & $+$0.20 & Spike \\
Llama-3.1-8B$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.57 & 0.85 & $+$0.38 & $+$0.36 & Spike \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3$^\dagger$ & 4:1 & 0.22 & 0.18 & $+$0.10 & $+$0.13 & Flat \\
Gemma-2-9B$^\ddagger$ & 2:1 & 0.23 & 0.18 & $+$0.13 & $+$0.15 & Flat \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_head_delta_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Per-head 2-bit quantization sensitivity across five architectures. Qwen2.5-7B shows high concentration in Layer-0 heads (``spread'' pattern); Yi-1.5-9B shows a single extreme outlier at Layer-4 Head-3 (``spike'' pattern); Llama-3.1-8B shows a dominant outlier at Layer-2 Head-5 (49\% of total distortion, ``spike'' pattern); Mistral-7B-v0.3 shows near-zero sensitivity across all heads; Gemma-2-9B exhibits the most uniform distribution, consistent with its low GQA ratio (2:1). Color intensity indicates PPL increase when the head is quantized to 2-bit.}
\label{fig:heatmap}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the per-head 2-bit distortion as a heatmap.
The contrast is stark: Qwen's Layer-0 heads show high distortion (dark cells) while mid-to-deep layers are near-zero; Yi-1.5 shows a single bright spot at Layer-4 Head-3 (34\% of total delta) with the remaining 191 heads near-uniform---a ``spike'' that MCKP cannot exploit; Gemma-2 exhibits the most uniform heatmap across its 336 heads, consistent with its 0.23 concentration; Mistral shows similarly low distortion across all layers and heads.

\subsection{Diagnostic Framework}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$, low $t_1/t_5$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. Mistral (0.22, $t_1/t_5{=}0.18$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.18$): counterproductive.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.
Both thresholds are illustrative, derived from five models; they should be validated on a broader set before being treated as general rules.
The diagnostic adds no computational overhead: it reuses the profiling data already required for the allocation solver and avoids wasted optimization effort on architectures where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.
